description_full: LATAM Airlines Group S.A., together with its subsidiaries, provides passenger and cargo air transportation services in Chile, Argentina, Peru, Colombia, Ecuador, Brazil, the United States, other Latin American countries, the Caribbean, Europe, and Oceania. As of December 31, 2024, the company provides passenger transport services to 160 destinations in 27 countries; and operated 371 fleet of aircraft. The company was formerly known as LAN Airlines S.A. and changed its name to LATAM Airlines Group S.A. in June 2012. LATAM Airlines Group S.A. was founded in 1929 and is headquartered in Santiago, Chile.

financial_summary: LATAM Airlines Group S.A. is a large-cap industrials business with a $13.5B market cap on $14.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +15% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 24% against a 9% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 21% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $2.0B in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.55× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 3.2×.

Management returns a meaningful 7.6% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 16% operating margin runs 8pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.47x).
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.5% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 8% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 10% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 33% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 46% and a beta of 0.90, it moves roughly with the market.
About $38.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
val: The stock trades 78% below its DCF fair value of $218, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $163 to $293 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 8.4 vs 24.1, EV/EBITDA 5.5 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 6.9 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 14.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 11.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 10 covering analysts target $72.36 on average, 53% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 11.7% annual cash-flow growth, 22pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 24% clears the cost of capital of 9.1% by 14pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 12.01).
It runs a 21% gross margin and converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.55x.
Operating margin is running 29pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.4x net debt to EBITDA ($2.2B of cash against $8.1B of debt), with interest covered 3.2x.
The current ratio of 0.60 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 15.1% over 3 years and 29.5% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 39%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 33.9% on average.
Analysts expect 40.4% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 9%.
It returns 7.6% a year to shareholders (4.3% in buybacks and 3.2% in dividends).
people: With about 43,972 employees, each generates about $324K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 5.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $45K of free cash flow per employee.
